newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Nigeria says its move to civil rule is irreversible.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria says its move to civil rule is irreversible.

text.p: Nigeria's Foreign Minister, Chief Tom Ikimi, said on Thursday his country was making steady progress in a transition to democracy and asked the United Nations to acknowledge what he called "positive developments."

"Political parties have now been registered and full political activities have resumed nationwide. Our transition to civil rule is now fully on an irreversible course," he said in a speech to the U.N. General Assembly.

Nigeria has been ruled mostly by military governments since independence from Britain in 1960. Its present ruler, General Sani Abacha, who seized power in 1993 after the annulment of presidential elections, has promised to restore civilian rule by October 1998.

Ikimi said a resolution which the Assembly adopted last December on the human rights situation in Nigeria was "based largely on media reporting and without any investigation of the facts of the matter."

He was referring to a resolution which condemned the "arbitrary execution, after a flawed judicial process" of writer Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other activists who had campaigned for compensation for the people of Ogoniland, in the southeast of the country, for oil produced there by multinational companies.
The executions resulted in Nigeria's suspension from the Commonwealth, which groups Britain and its former colonies, and arms embargoes by the European Union and the United States.

Ikimi said despite Nigeria's unhappiness with the Assembly resolution, adopted by a vote of 101 to 14 with 47 abstentions, it invited the United Nations to send a fact-finding mission "which identified areas of progress in our domestic situation (and) also made constructive recommendations."

He thanked those governments which did not support the Assembly resolution and said a number of countries "have reconsidered their position on the matter in favour of Nigeria" since the U.N. mission's visit.

Urging the Assembly to "take cognizance of these positive developments," he said: "The present administration in my country has continued to make steady progress in the implementation of its programme of transition to democratic rule."

Citing local government elections last March, he said the "impressive turnout of voters nation-wide and the general atmosphere of tranquility" had elicited goodwill and support both inside and outside the country.
On the question of the election of a secretary-general, Ikimi strongly supported a second five-year term for Boutros Boutros-Ghali, whose re-election is opposed by the United States.

He said Boutros-Ghali, whose current term expires at the end of this year, had shown "uncommon and unrelenting commitment to the challenges of his office" and deserved gratitude and continued support.

Noting the Egyptian diplomat was the only candidate recommended by the Organisation of African Unity, Ikimi said: "Like his predecessors, Dr Boutros Boutros-Ghali should be given a second term to serve our organisation. It is the only credible thing to do. For us, this is a matter of principle."
